What to know about the Iran war today:
- Three Saudi citizens were killed Thursday in an attack by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Riyadh's main airport. Fighting between the Iranian proxy group and Saudi-backed forces in Yemen has escalated this week in what appears to be the new epicenter of the wider .
- Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Thursday that Tehran had revised its proposals to initiate peace talks with the U.S. and stood ready to finalize them through mediators. President Trump rejected a "7-day plan" offered by Iran in late September to get both sides back around the negotiating table.
- The price of Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, eased Friday to around $103 a barrel after Mr. Trump promised the U.S. would not resume attacks on Iran before the U.S. midterm elections early next month. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he offered no specifics.
Trump says Iran can either "give us everything or they don't exist any longer"
During a rally in upstate New York, President Trump said, "Iran will be very quick, one way or the other. Either they give us everything, or they don't exist any longer. They know that"
The president made the comments while criticizing the Nobel Peace Prize committee for not awarding him the prize — a frequent complaint by Mr. Trump. Calling the body "crooked," Mr. Trump attacked it for giving the prize to former International Criminal Court Judge Navanethem Pillay, whom the president called a "mystery person."
"This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision," he said. "The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization."
Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed more than 100 Houthi targets
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said Saturday it destroyed more than 100 military targets in a "large-scale operation" against the Iran-backed group.
"We are carrying out a large-scale operation targeting the personnel and capabilities of the Houthi terrorist militia," Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi coalition, wrote on X.
"We destroyed 136 military targets in areas controlled by the Houthi terrorist militia," he said in a separate post.
The Houthi's Almasirah TV channel reported that Saudi missiles targeted areas in the northwestern Yemeni governorate of Saada.
The conflict between the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government — which Saudi Arabia supports — reignited in July, and has since spilled over into the neighboring kingdom.
In addition to seizing territory along the Red Sea coast in Yemen, the Houthis have attacked transport hubs, oil facilities and other civilian targets in the world's largest crude exporter with drones and missiles.
Trump says Russia will release millions of tons of diesel
President Trump said Russia has agreed to provide the world with millions of tons of diesel fuel over the next several months in a bid to decrease skyrocketing global prices.
In a Truth Social post, the president said he had just gotten off the phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who had agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel immediately. He said another 500,000 tons of diesel would be released in November, followed by 1 million tons in December.
"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Mr. Trump continued.
The Treasury Department also announced Friday that it would temporarily waive sanctions on Russia's energy sector to "allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
Mr. Trump had earlier Friday teased a "big announcement coming up on diesel" during remarks at a Columbus Day celebration.
Diesel prices have skyrocketed in recent months amid the war with Iran. The average price of a gallon of diesel is $6.28, according to AAA, which is up from $5.94 a month ago and $3.68 a year ago.

Mr. Trump pointed out Energy Secretary Chris Wright and said he was "doing a great job."
"We have, I think, some big news on that diesel situation," the president said. "It's gonna — we're gonna be knocking the hell out of it. And remember, what have we done? We stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon. That's big time. And the prices — the prices will come tumbling."
Diesel prices have skyrocketed in recent months amid the war with Iran. The average price of a gallon of diesel is $6.28, according to AAA, which is up from $5.94 a month ago and $3.68 a year ago.
Diesel had never previously crossed $6 a gallon until just before Labor Day weekend. The record, hit on Sept. 22, was $6.53 per gallon. Diesel is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, so it's a factor for nearly every type of good, including groceries.
The Trump administration has looked into several ways to lower diesel prices, most recently signing an executive order this week allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on highways. Red-dyed diesel is exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon that applies to regular diesel.
Sri Lanka has no plans to help 19 Iranian tankers stuck due to blockade, foreign ministry says
Sri Lanka's government says it has no immediate plans to help 19 Iranian ships that have been anchored in the international waters near the island nation facing food, water and fuel shortages.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Thushara Rodrigo said Sri Lanka will put its national interest first before considering any help, and the companies that supply ships are aware of possible secondary sanctions from the United States.
He said, however, there hasn't been any communication from the U.S. warning of repercussions should Sri Lanka decide to help.
Rodrigo said the ships are stationed 24 nautical miles from Sri Lanka's coast and have reported shortages of food, water and fuel.
Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath told local Sunday Times newspaper the ships are Iranian oil tankers and they have been anchored off Sri Lanka for the past several months after the U.S. resumed its naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving dozens of Iranian vessels stranded and unable to return home.
U.K., France, Germany, Australia and Canada advise against travel to Saudi Arabia after attacks
The U.K., France, Germany, Australia and Canada have advised their citizens against travel to parts of Saudi Arabia following a wave of Houthi attacks, including one that killed three civilians at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Thursday.
The U.K. Foreign Office now advises against all but essential travel to the Riyadh region, Najran, Jizan and Aseer provinces, Taif city and Taif International Airport, and against all travel within six miles of the Yemeni border.
France says travel to Najran, Abha, Khamis Muhsait and Djizan in the south of the kingdom "remains strongly discouraged," and Germany, Australia and Canada have all advised against all travel to the country.
The U.S. has also tightened restrictions, requiring government employees to obtain special authorization to use Riyadh airport, and barring them from all travel within 20 miles of the Yemen border. U.S. government employees also require "special authorization for travel to the provinces of Jizan, Asir, Najran, and the cities of Qatif, Yanbu, and Taif."
There is currently no warning for U.S. nationals more broadly to avoid Saudi Arabia, but the U.S. embassy in Riyadh urged Americans across the Middle East to "exercise heightened vigilance due to the complex security environment."
Yemen's Saudi-backed military claims it has taken back Bab el-Mandeb Strait
Yemeni government forces, backed by air support from the Saudi-led coalition, have taken control of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Mayyun Island from the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, a Saudi diplomat said Friday.
Saudi Arabian Ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed Al Jaber, said in a post on X that the strait had been "cleansed" of remaining Houthi forces.
Fighting escalated dramatically this week after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive to retake territory held by Houthis, including some coastline around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that was seized by the rebels only weeks ago. The Houthis have held a vast portion of Yemen, including its capital Sanaa, for over a decade.
Yemeni forces claimed earlier this week to have retaken other key territory along the Red Sea coast, north of the strait, but the Houthis insisted Tuesday that their fighters still had "full control over all their gains on the ground."

The Iran-backed Houthis appeared to taunt Saudi Arabia on Friday, as the group's spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree declared that humanitarian flights to and from Riyadh's airport would be allowed only with authorization from the Yemeni rebel group.

articles.title: Iran turns on Pakistan as Saudi defense pact takes effect - Iran International
articles.summary: Iran turns on Pakistan as Saudi defense pact takes effect  Iran InternationalAs Munir's military takes on Gulf role, Pakistan's parliament is not involved  ReutersPakistan’s Yemen moment  DawnPakistan confirms it has troops in Saudi as conflict with Yemen’s Houthi rebels escalates  CNNTurkey Says It Won’t Deploy Troops for Attacks Under Mecca Pact  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
Iran has sharpened its criticism of a Saudi Arabia-Pakistan-Turkey defense pact after it became operational, warning against intervention in Yemen and questioning Pakistan’s role as a mediator between Tehran and Washington.
The trilateral pact entered its operational phase on October 5 following an escalation in Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi infrastructure. Turkey and Pakistan said they had begun taking measures to support Saudi Arabia.
Under arrangements discussed by the three countries, Pakistani and Turkish forces are expected to provide military, technical and intelligence support to Saudi Arabia, including defensive capabilities inside the kingdom. Officials have said the forces will not take part in offensive operations in Yemen.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, asked on Sunday about reports that tens of thousands of Pakistani troops could be deployed to Saudi Arabia, said: “We have also heard this rumor, and we hope it is not true.”
“The countries of the region are well aware that any intervention in the Yemen issue could have undesirable consequences for the region,” he added, expressing hope that pacts such as the Mecca agreement would not be used “against the interests and welfare of the Muslim community.”
The Saudi Arabia-Turkey-Pakistan defense pact, signed in August in Mecca, stipulates that an attack on any one of the three countries will be treated as an attack on all three.
‘Begging for security’
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, without directly referring to the pact, called on neighboring countries to pursue “self-reliance” and a policy based on “genuine brotherhood.” He also said such agreements would not constrain Iran.
Several lawmakers dismissed the pact as largely symbolic. Ahmad Bakhshayesh, a member of parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, called it a “paper and political pact.”
Sharper criticism came from committee member Ebrahim Rezaei.
“The Saudis should know that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan will not bring them security, just as years of one-sided milking of the Americans did not bring them security,” he wrote on X. “Correct your policies so that you do not have to beg others for security.”
That tone has hardened as the pact has moved into its operational phase.
Alaeddin Boroujerdi, a member of parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said Thursday that Turkish and Pakistani involvement in the Saudi conflict with Ansarullah, as the Houthis are formally known, would neither weaken the group nor restrict its ability to operate in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
“The entry of Pakistan and Turkey will definitely work to their own detriment,” he told ISNA. “They should learn from history ... Saudi Arabia once had a coalition with a large number of countries, but after seven years of war in Yemen, it was defeated.”
‘Regional intervenor’
Iranian criticism has focused more heavily on Pakistan than Turkey, in large part because of Islamabad’s prominent role in mediating between Tehran and Washington.
Lawmaker Ahmad Naderi wrote on X that “Pakistan’s entry alongside Saudi Arabia into the war against the people of Yemen … shows that Pakistan should no longer be considered a mediator but a regional intervenor.”
The Tabnak news website went further, saying Iran viewed the deployment of Pakistani forces to Saudi Arabia as a threat to its security and “will not tolerate Pakistan’s military presence for military operations in the Yemen war.”
It also warned that Pakistan’s increasingly overt alignment with Saudi Arabia could heighten sectarian tensions at home and bring instability to the Iranian-Pakistani border.
Conservative commentator Hassan Hanizadeh similarly accused Saudi Arabia of seeking to create a religious divide, describing a recent meeting in Riyadh involving Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials as a sign of “the formation of a Shiite-Sunni polarization in the region.”
Boroujerdi pointed to potential domestic opposition in Pakistan, saying its people were “revolutionary, Muslim and highly sensitive to such issues” and that Islamabad would not have an easy path if it entered the war.
‘Alliance against the oppressed?’
Iranian state media have adopted a more confrontational tone as the pact has become operational, while giving extensive coverage to warnings from Houthi officials directed at Turkey and Pakistan.
Tasnim described the development as “Turkey and Pakistan join the Saudi war against the Yemeni people,” while Nour News, which is close to Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, asked: “Mecca alliance or alliance against the oppressed people of Yemen?!”
In a Thursday commentary, Tasnim warned that if Ankara and Islamabad participate in attacks on Yemen, “they may be directly harmed through attacks on their ships, interests and perhaps even their own territory.”

articles.title: US sanctions on ICC spark global backlash, European calls for action
articles.summary: The U.S. faced mounting international criticism Friday over its sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), as European governments, Canada and Japan rallied...
articles.full_text:
The U.S. faced mounting international criticism Friday over its sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), as European governments, Canada and Japan rallied behind the tribunal and warned that Washington's move threatened international justice and judicial independence.
In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands and the U.K., alongside their counterparts from Canada and Japan, expressed strong opposition to the sanctions, warning of serious consequences for the court's operations and personnel.
"We, the undersigned States Parties to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC), reaffirm our continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC," the ministers said.
They cautioned that the restrictions, if implemented, would significantly affect the tribunal's work, its employees and their families, while welcoming preparations aimed at maintaining its operations.
The eight countries pledged to maintain dialogue with nations outside the Rome Statute, the treaty establishing the ICC, ahead of the Assembly of States Parties in December.
"We will continue to work together to support the Court's vital work, uphold the rules-based international system, and advance accountability," they said.
The ICC itself denounced the measures as an attempt to obstruct justice and intimidate those cooperating with the tribunal.
The sanctions represent "an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order," the court said, warning that they undermine the principle that no individual is above the law.
The tribunal vowed to continue its work despite the restrictions but urged its member states to defend its independence.
"The Court, for its part, will not be deterred," it said, adding that its future also depended on the governments that established it.
The European Commission similarly criticized Washington's decision and pledged to consider measures to protect the tribunal and European businesses affected by the sanctions.
"The EU stands ready to take any necessary measures to enable the Court to carry out its work," the commission said, referring to investigations and prosecutions involving war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen described the sanctions as deeply regrettable but emphasized that a six-month period before their implementation would allow time for negotiations.
"We will stand firm in defence of the Court," he said, adding that service providers could continue working with the tribunal during the transition period.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot called for more decisive European action, urging the EU to activate its Blocking Statute to shield the court from the effects of U.S. sanctions.
"Europe must act," Prevot said, announcing plans to raise the issue with EU foreign ministers and at the upcoming European Council meeting.
German Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig also condemned the decision, highlighting Washington's historic role in establishing international criminal accountability following World War II.
She recalled that the United States had championed the Nuremberg trials against senior Nazi officials, helping lay the foundations of modern international criminal law.
"It is utterly staggering that the US, of all countries, is now setting out to destroy this idea once and for all," Hubig said.
In Washington, Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, called the sanctions "unfortunate and short-sighted," accusing the Trump administration of further isolating the United States and undermining efforts to prosecute atrocities in Ukraine and Darfur.
Human rights organizations also criticized the measures, linking them to Washington's opposition to ICC proceedings involving U.S. and Israeli officials.
Philippe Bolopion, executive director of Human Rights Watch, accused the Trump administration of seeking to dismantle the tribunal to protect American and Israeli officials from potential prosecution.
He urged governments, particularly the EU, to take immediate steps to protect the ICC, its employees and those cooperating with its investigations.
James A. Goldston, executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, similarly described the sanctions as a deliberate challenge to judicial independence and equality before the law.
He characterized the move as part of a broader effort to weaken the international justice system.
The sanctions have intensified tensions between Washington and its European allies over the ICC, which has faced U.S. criticism over its investigations involving American personnel and arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

articles.title: ICC condemns sweeping US sanctions as assault on international law
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday condemned sweeping U.S. sanctions targeting the tribunal, calling them an attack on the foundations of international law and warnin...
articles.full_text:
The International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday condemned sweeping U.S. sanctions targeting the tribunal, calling them an attack on the foundations of international law and warning that history would judge efforts to undermine its independence.
The measures represent "an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order," the court said in a statement, stressing that no individual should be above the law.
The Trump administration announced sanctions against the ICC on Friday, hours after a former judge at the tribunal was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, setting the stage for renewed diplomatic tensions between Washington and its European allies.
Unlike previous restrictions targeting individual judges and prosecutors, the latest measures could penalize companies and financial institutions providing services to the court, potentially disrupting its operations.
"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement first reported by Reuters.
"That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," he added.
ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan denounced the decision, saying the restrictions were designed to weaken international justice but would not prevent the tribunal from carrying out its mandate.
"The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing," Khan told Reuters.
"Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions," she added.
Washington has repeatedly criticized the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other Israeli officials over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during Israel's genocidal military offensive in Gaza.
Established in 2002 to prosecute genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, the Hague-based tribunal has 125 member states, including all European Union countries and every NATO member except the United States and Türkiye.
The court has historically received strong support from European governments, many of which are close U.S. allies.
Nobel recognition highlights pressure on international justice
The sanctions announcement came shortly after South African jurist Navi Pillay, who served on the ICC's Appeals Chamber from 2003 to 2008, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
The Nobel committee said the decision was intended to draw attention to growing political pressure on international judicial institutions.
In its citation, the committee said the award sought to "issue a reminder" at a time when judges and international legal bodies were facing political attacks.
"An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world," the committee said.
The timing of the award and Washington's announcement underscored tensions over the authority and independence of international courts.
US grants limited exemptions as ICC prepares for disruption
Despite the broad restrictions, the U.S. Treasury Department issued four general licenses shortly after the announcement, allowing certain transactions involving telecommunications, software, pension payments and ICC detainees to continue.
U.S. sanctions generally prohibit American companies from conducting business with designated organizations, potentially forcing banks to close accounts, insurers to withdraw coverage and technology providers to suspend services.
The Trump administration previously sanctioned individual ICC officials during the president's first term. Those restrictions were lifted under former President Joe Biden.
Washington imposed additional sanctions shortly after Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
Anticipating broader measures, ICC officials have spent months preparing contingency arrangements, including replacing Microsoft software with open-source alternatives and securing new banking and health insurance services.
Earlier this week, ICC Registrar Osvaldo Zavala Giler urged the European Union to consider activating its blocking mechanism, a legal instrument intended to protect European entities from the extraterritorial effects of foreign sanctions.
Rubio said Washington had postponed the latest measures to allow ICC member states to address U.S. objections, but those efforts had failed to produce an acceptable outcome.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," Rubio said, urging U.S. allies that belong to the tribunal to intervene.
He added that Washington expected countries relying on American military support to help restrain the court's activities.
The secretary of state said the sanctions were structured to leave room for negotiations with countries party to the Rome Statute, the treaty establishing the ICC.
"We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns. If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly," Rubio said.
The court, however, maintained that its investigations and prosecutions would continue despite the restrictions, reaffirming its commitment to pursuing accountability for serious international crimes.

Thousands of Palestinian families remain desperate for answers about loved ones who disappeared during three years of Israeli attacks on Gaza, as widespread destruction, restricted access and limited forensic resources hamper efforts to find the missing.
The United Nations estimates that millions of tonnes of debris cover Gaza, while Palestinian Civil Defense says more than 8,000 people remain missing beneath the rubble. Others may have been detained or remain unaccounted for, leaving families uncertain whether their relatives are alive or dead.
Pat Griffiths, spokesperson for the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in Jerusalem, described seeing families gather at hospitals when buses carrying released Palestinian detainees arrive in Gaza. Some hold photographs of missing relatives, hoping to discover whether they are among those released.
Psychologists call this experience "ambiguous loss," a form of grief in which families cannot establish whether their loved ones are alive or dead.
"You don't know if your loved one you haven't heard from ... is alive or if they've been killed. You don't know if they're detained or not," Griffiths told Anadolu Agency (AA).
"Thousands of people live with this limbo. This pain of not knowing what to do or how to feel exactly. They're stuck."
Amani Al Naouq, an ICRC spokesperson in Gaza, said families repeatedly approach the organization seeking answers.
"If they are dead, we can be relieved. But the fact that we don't know if they are dead or alive," she recalled families saying. "That's one of the most difficult things for them."
Some continue contacting the ICRC even when answers are unavailable, simply needing somewhere to share their anguish. Others begin accepting that missing relatives have died without receiving confirmation, Al Naouq said.
The search is complicated by the scale of destruction across Gaza, where rubble may contain human remains, unexploded ordnance and evidence relevant to investigations into alleged international crimes.
An April 2026 damage assessment by the European Union, United Nations and World Bank estimated that removing and managing more than 68 million metric tons of debris would cost more than $1.7 billion.
Al Naouq said recovery teams have extremely limited heavy machinery, sometimes relying on just one or two excavators rented from private suppliers. Much of the work is performed with smaller equipment or by hand.
Teams also depend on families to identify where missing relatives were last seen, including specific buildings and rooms. Recounting those moments can force relatives to relive their inability to rescue loved ones.
"It's actually back again an open wound for these families," Al Naouq said.
Griffiths, who recently spent a week in Gaza, described seeing kilometers of rubble, much of it posing dangers from unexploded remnants of war. The ICRC supports the rental of two excavators, but he said the contribution was minimal compared with the need.
"The scale of the task ahead of them, it's daunting. It's huge," he said.
Restricted access prevents recovery teams from safely reaching large areas. DNA testing is also unavailable in Gaza, according to the ICRC, forcing forensic specialists to rely on details such as age, height, dental information, clothing, previous injuries and personal belongings.
Time further complicates identification as remains decompose and rubble movement separates them from their original locations.
"The more time passes, the harder identifying the deceased gets," Griffiths said, warning that searches can continue for decades, as seen in conflicts in Syria, Iraq, Afghanistan and the Balkans.
Mayy El Sheikh, of the U.N. Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory, recalled interviewing a 37-year-old woman with a disability whose husband disappeared during an attack on his family's home in northern Gaza in 2023. The couple have a 5-year-old son.
Almost everyone in her husband's family was killed. Some bodies were recovered, but his remains were not, El Sheikh said.
The woman believes she knows where he lies beneath the rubble but cannot reach the site because it is beyond the deployment line for Israeli forces, known as the "yellow line."
El Sheikh said the woman felt unable to help her son recover because he had no grave to visit. She also believed she had failed her husband by being unable to recover his remains and honor him through burial.
"For her, the war is not over until her husband is found," El Sheikh said.
Other families have believed missing relatives were dead before recognizing them alive in photographs or videos from Israeli prisons, she added.
The destruction of Gaza's ruins has raised concerns that human remains and evidence of alleged international crimes could disappear.
Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, has warned that removing, crushing and relocating rubble in areas under Israeli military control could destroy evidence.
El Sheikh said restricted access, reported debris removal and limited forensic resources have increased the risk that evidence is being lost or damaged. Large areas remain inaccessible to independent observers and investigators.
She also cited reports of remains being returned to Palestinian authorities without identifying information or details about where they were recovered.
"They have returned remains to the Palestinian authorities, sometimes even partial remains with no identification and no clarity on where they were recovered or how they were killed," she said.
Srinivasan Muralidhar, chair of the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, said the commission had received reports of rubble removal that could destroy evidence.
"We are concerned that the removal of rubble could result in evidence getting lost forever," he said.
Evidence recovered from destroyed buildings can complement witness testimony, medical records and forensic findings, helping investigators reconstruct events. Although losing evidence would not necessarily prevent investigations into alleged crimes, Muralidhar said, it could leave important gaps.
He also emphasized families' right to know what happened to their relatives.
"In international law, there is a known concept of the right to the truth. Every family wants to know what exactly happened," he said.
Griffiths called for more heavy machinery, greater humanitarian access and safe passage for recovery teams to reach areas currently beyond their reach.
Muralidhar urged international cooperation to accelerate debris removal while protecting potential evidence and preventing further destruction.
"We have to have cooperation across countries to help clear the rubble quicker," he said, warning that continued attacks could make recovery increasingly difficult.
The ICRC has supported a cemetery for unidentified dead in Deir al-Balah, where recovered remains can be buried individually while information is preserved for future identification.
Forensic teams document available identifying details and assign each unidentified person a unique serial number linked to their burial record. The ICRC is also supporting an information-sharing system connecting recovery teams, forensic authorities and cemetery administrators.
The effort could enable future identification if DNA testing becomes available in Gaza.
During a visit to the cemetery, Griffiths and Al Naouq met a young woman whose husband's remains had been identified using available forensic methods.
"She could visit his grave, she could stand at his grave, to be near him," Griffiths said, describing the closure the burial provided.

articles.title: 31 civilians killed in RSF drone strike on Sudan displacement camp
articles.summary: At least 31 civilians were killed and 19 others were wounded when a drone strike blamed on Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) hit a camp for displaced people in southe...
articles.full_text:
At least 31 civilians were killed and 19 others were wounded when a drone strike blamed on Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) hit a camp for displaced people in southeastern Blue Nile state, a local medical group said Friday.
In a statement, the Sudan Doctors Network said the attack targeted a gathering of displaced people in the Abu Shandi area of Wad Al-Mahi locality.
The group said four children were among those killed, while six children and eight women were among the injured.
It condemned the attack, saying the victims were unarmed civilians who had fled the conflict in search of safety.
The network described the strike as a war crime and a violation of international humanitarian law, holding the RSF responsible.
It called on the U.N., humanitarian agencies and international human rights organizations to urgently condemn the attack and take action to protect civilians.
There was no immediate comment from the RSF on the allegations.
Blue Nile state has witnessed escalating violence in recent weeks, with the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), launching attacks in several areas.
On Oct. 3, Sudanese authorities accused the RSF of carrying out drone strikes targeting the governor’s residence and civilian sites in Damazin, the state capital.
Sudan has been engulfed in fighting between the army and the RSF since April 2023, leaving tens of thousands dead and around 13 million displaced, according to U.N. and international estimates.

articles.title: Magnitude 7.6 earthquake rocks Panama, tremors reach Colombia
articles.summary: A magnitude 7.6 earthquake jolted Panama on Friday morning, forcing evacuations as buildings swayed in the capital and tremors spread across the border into neighboring Colombia. T...
articles.full_text:
A magnitude 7.6 earthquake jolted Panama on Friday morning, forcing evacuations as buildings swayed in the capital and tremors spread across the border into neighboring Colombia.
The quake was centered about 10 kilometers (6 miles) southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, the U.S. Geological Survey said. It struck at a depth of 10 kilometers (6 miles).
Visibly shaken residents of Panama City gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact on Friday.
"We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we’re okay, though we’re very scared," Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, where the earthquake struck, told The Associated Press by phone. "Everyone is outside, scared.”
Aftershocks continued to shake the streets on Friday shortly after the quake. The National Weather Service issued a tsunami warning Friday for the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Nicaragua and Guatemala.
Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino called for calm on Friday, writing on X: "What happened should not be used to cause alarm or disorder.”
Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said on the Telemetro Reporta news channel that damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos. He said there were no reports of damage in the capital, which is known for its hundreds of skyscrapers.
Video aired by local news outlets showed a Catholic cathedral collapsing and part of a hotel’s facade falling onto a car in the city of Penonomé, in the central province of Coclé. No casualties were immediately reported.
Panama lies along the "Ring of Fire," a 40,000-kilometer (25,000-mile) arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world’s earthquakes occur.
Panama's Civil Protection said it was investigating possible damage in regions near the epicenter.

Zacharia did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but if she accepts the role, she would fill a critical role in the Trump administration before next month's midterm congressional elections.

Zacharia briefly served as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security before departing in March.
The conservative commentator is a senior communications adviser for Truth Social and the Trump Media & Technology Group, according to her LinkedIn page.
Zacharia previously worked as a legal adviser for Fix California, a conservative group that aims to address what it described as "the left’s stranglehold" on state politics. articles.title: Trump sparks backlash with anti-Somali, anti-Muslim rhetoric
articles.summary: In a fresh outburst of anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric, President Donald Trump portrayed Minnesota’s Somali American community as a threat to the state Thursday, hours after b...
articles.full_text:
In a fresh outburst of anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric, President Donald Trump portrayed Minnesota’s Somali American community as a threat to the state Thursday, hours after branding Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate, a radical extremist.
“The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants. There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State. The people of Minnesota must fight back,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Trump also called on Minnesota authorities to seek federal intervention.
Civil rights advocates have criticized the Republican president’s rhetoric toward minorities and immigrants, including his previous characterization of Somalis as “garbage.”
Trump has repeatedly cited a Minnesota fraud scandal dating to 2020, in which dozens of people were accused of defrauding a state-run, federally funded child nutrition program of millions of dollars. Many of the defendants were Somali Americans.
In May, Aimee Bock, who is not a Somali immigrant and led the Minnesota nonprofit involved in the scandal, was sentenced to 41 years in prison after being convicted last year of orchestrating the scheme.
Trump has used the fraud case to justify targeting Minnesota, a Democratic-led state, with an aggressive immigration enforcement operation earlier this year. He has also pursued measures aimed at restricting social service programs in the state, including Medicaid and child care.
Rights groups have accused Trump of using individual fraud cases to justify collectively targeting immigrant communities. They have also criticized his approach to combating fraud, pointing to his pardons of people convicted of fraud.
“Somali Minnesotans are our neighbors. They are part of Minnesota. And the Minnesota I know and love is so much better than this bigotry,” Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said in response to Trump’s post.
In another post late Wednesday, Trump called El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, a “RADICAL Extremist” and “Terrorist Sympathizer” while endorsing Republican candidate Mike Rogers.
Democrats said Trump’s rhetoric was intended to distract voters from the impact of his policies ahead of the November U.S. midterm elections.
“He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor’s office,” El-Sayed, who has faced anti-Muslim attacks from other Republicans, said Thursday.
The Michigan Democratic Party and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer described Trump’s rhetoric as desperate and racist.
Trump has previously targeted minority communities with his rhetoric, including by spreading false claims that Haitian immigrants in an Ohio town were eating pets and using the term “Palestinian” as an insult.

articles.title: Burnham’s Labour holds off Greens in London election test
articles.summary: Labour won the parliamentary by-election in the central London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras on Friday, defeating a strong challenge from the left-wing Green Party in a bo...
articles.full_text:
Labour won the parliamentary by-election in the central London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras on Friday, defeating a strong challenge from the left-wing Green Party in a boost for Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, the local council leader, secured 12,292 votes, beating Green Party leader Zack Polanski, who received 8,928. The seat became vacant after former Labour leader Keir Starmer stepped down as a lawmaker.
The expected victory will strengthen Burnham's position after lawmakers installed him as prime minister amid concerns that Starmer's unpopularity was leaving Labour vulnerable to a challenge from the populist Reform UK party at the next general election.
After losing left-wing support to the Greens earlier this year, Labour appears to have won back many voters, raising further questions about Polanski's leadership. He had promised to make his party an "eco-populist" movement.
The 43-year-old former actor and hypnotherapist, who had some success in drawing voters away from Labour before Burnham came to power, has come under fire after party members passed a motion titled "Zionism Is Racism."
The motion called for "the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine" and was criticized by Jewish groups, other parties and most Green Party lawmakers.
After the fiercely contested vote, Polanski, who did not vote on the motion, responded to his critics by saying he would stay on as leader. He described the by-election result as part of "Andy Burnham's honeymoon."
However, he did not receive a full endorsement from the party's former leader, Caroline Lucas, who struggled to contain her anger over what she described as his lack of leadership on the Zionism motion at last week's annual conference.
Asked whether Polanski should remain leader, Lucas told the BBC: "I think just let's see what happens in the coming days and weeks."
"I want him to speak now about what has happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday."
Abdi-Wali, who arrived in Britain as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a defeat for "those who seek to divide us."
"We have a responsibility to defend what we've built and pass it on," she said. "Throughout our campaign, we chose hope, and the people of Holborn and St Pancras chose it with us. And now it's time to deliver."
The by-election was an early test for Burnham, whose predecessor, Starmer, stepped down as a lawmaker in September after being ousted as prime minister in July.
Under Starmer, Labour had also ceded ground to the Green Party, which made record gains in London in May's local elections as its appeal grew among younger, left-leaning voters in the capital and other urban areas.
The Greens have since fallen back in opinion polls after Burnham made policy proposals that strengthened Labour's standing among left-leaning voters, including a tougher line on Israel and a more ambitious approach to relations with the European Union.
Polanski, who is Jewish, was repeatedly questioned after the by-election about the conference vote on Zionism. The Green Party leader again appeared to distance himself from the motion, saying only that he believed the displacement of Palestinians and what he called an "ongoing genocide" were racist.
For now, he said, the Green Party should direct its challenge at Burnham's Labour Party and focus on whether the governing party's budget on Oct. 28 delivers on its promises.
"So many people told me on the doorstep that they want to give Andy Burnham a chance," Polanski told broadcasters. "Well, he's got a chance now. Let's see what he does with it."

articles.title: Zelenskyy blasts US over Russia ties as strikes kill 78 in Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the United States of being unwilling to help Ukraine after Russian strikes killed 78 people and wounded 215 across the country in tw...
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the United States of being unwilling to help Ukraine after Russian strikes killed 78 people and wounded 215 across the country in two days, urging President Donald Trump to increase military support and sanctions against Moscow.
The attacks included a devastating strike on the eastern city of Kramatorsk, where at least 35 people were killed and 20 wounded, according to Ukrainian officials.
The bombardment followed a major Russian drone and missile assault a day earlier that killed dozens, including 22 people in a residential building in Pryluky, about 130 kilometers (80 miles) east of Kyiv.
Speaking to reporters Thursday in Pryluky, Zelenskyy criticized Washington for pursuing potential economic cooperation with Russia while attempting to mediate the war, now in its fifth year.
He also called on the United States to expand Ukraine's access to the Starlink satellite communications network, saying it could help Ukrainian forces identify and target Russian ballistic missile launchers.
"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran," Zelenskyy said. "Give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table."
The Ukrainian leader questioned U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's assessment earlier Thursday that the war had reached a stalemate and Washington would continue working toward a settlement.
Zelenskyy argued that Washington's pursuit of economic projects with Moscow contradicted claims that diplomatic progress had stalled.
"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said.
"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," he added.
His remarks followed a Reuters report that senior Russian and U.S. officials, including U.S. Special Envoy Jared Kushner, had discussed bringing an American investor into the Nord Stream pipeline network, which transported Russian natural gas to Germany before Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelenskyy urged Trump to increase sanctions pressure on Russia, arguing that stronger support for Ukraine could help bring Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table.
Ukrainian negotiators are scheduled to travel to the United States on Friday and Saturday for talks. Zelenskyy said he expected European partners to join the discussions, with air defense expected to be a key issue amid continued Russian attacks.
In Kramatorsk, a Russian guided aerial bomb struck the city Thursday, killing dozens and damaging two buses. A subsequent drone attack killed two more people, bringing the reported death toll to 35.
Regional Governor Vadym Filashkin accused Russian forces of deliberately targeting civilians.
"The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible," he said on Telegram.
Images released by officials showed bodies scattered across a debris-covered street beside a charred bus. Some victims had not been identified, Zelenskyy said, warning that the attack would not go unanswered.
Elsewhere, a Russian guided aerial bomb killed two people in a village in southeastern Dnipropetrovsk region, while another person died in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk, local authorities said.
The latest bombardment followed Wednesday's attacks, which killed dozens across Ukraine, including 22 people in Pryluky.
Russia also attacked Kyiv on Thursday morning, killing four people and wounding 19, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The strikes disrupted water and electricity supplies in parts of the capital, with officials warning that restoring services would take time.
Moscow has intensified drone attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, targeting warehouses, data centers and other infrastructure while renewing its campaign against Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter.
Russian technology company Yandex said it could not yet determine whether equipment at a data center hit by a Ukrainian drone attack could be restored.
Zelenskyy did not specifically address the strike on Yandex but said Ukraine was mirroring Russian attacks on data centers.
Ukraine has sought to regain the battlefield initiative as Russian territorial advances have slowed this year. However, Moscow's sustained air campaign continues to threaten civilians, critical infrastructure and the country's energy security.

articles.title: Plague fears fuel online push for antibiotics, emergency kits
articles.summary: Reports that a woman working at a plague research institute in Russia’s Irkutsk region died from the disease have fueled a surge in online interest across North America in potentia...
articles.full_text:
Reports that a woman working at a plague research institute in Russia’s Irkutsk region died from the disease have fueled a surge in online interest across North America in potential treatments.
Russian authorities have not confirmed that the woman died of plague. The regional governor said Thursday that no health concerns had been identified after officials traced all her contacts.
Despite the lack of confirmation, social media influencers and doomsday preppers are promoting a $300 kit they claim can help people avoid emergency room visits.
“Don’t wait until everybody is scrambling. Prepare before you need it,” reads the caption of a Facebook video viewed more than 161,000 times and posted with the hashtags #Russia and #plague.
The posts include personalized discount codes, suggesting the creators may receive financial compensation when purchases are made.
The Wellness Company, a brand promoted in many of the videos, saw a subsequent spike in online searches, according to Google Trends data.
The company is fronted by Peter McCullough, an American cardiologist who has promoted COVID-19 conspiracy theories and health misinformation debunked by Agence France-Presse (AFP). The company did not immediately respond to questions about the kits.
Rogan O’Handley, known on social media as DC Draino, highlighted the kit’s inclusion of the antibiotic doxycycline to his 2.9 million followers.
Doxycycline is among the antibiotics used to treat plague in countries where cases occur each year, helping contain outbreaks.
“We know how to treat it,” said Isaac Bogoch, an infectious disease specialist at Toronto General Hospital.
“Obviously it can be a very severe infection,” he said, but he warned against taking a course of antibiotics without known exposure.
He said the unconfirmed case in Russia “isn’t the type of infection that would cause a pandemic.”
Paul Keim, a plague researcher and professor at Northern Arizona University, also said there was no reason for people in North America to start taking doxycycline.
“You’re altering the microbiome of your gut, and perhaps creating antibiotic-resistant bacteria in your body that will fight off the drug therapy the next time you really need it,” he said.
The kits are also advertised as containing “hard-to-find” prescription medications such as ivermectin.
But “ivermectin is never really used for a bacterial disease,” Keim said.
The antiparasitic drug is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to treat certain parasitic worm infections.
Yet it continues to be touted as a solution in health misinformation, in part because authorities rejected its use as an effective treatment for COVID-19 after clinical trials failed to demonstrate sufficient benefits.
This is not the first public health scare to prompt individuals to promote unproven medical solutions.
When a cruise ship passenger contracted the rare hantavirus in May, social media accounts also quickly touted ivermectin as a “cure,” even though there is no established treatment for the disease.
Amid the 2026 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, videos featuring a doctor recommending vitamin D3 and zinc spread through accounts selling supplements, despite the substances being unable to treat the disease.
“Whenever there is a crisis, especially in the health space, the grifters are gonna come out,” said Timothy Caulfield, a misinformation expert and professor at the University of Alberta.
“They exploit fear and uncertainty to sell unproven products.”

articles.title: UN warns over police force as French student protests intensify
articles.summary: The United Nations has expressed concern over police tactics during nationwide student protests in France, where more than 6,800 people have been detained and several injured as de...
articles.full_text:
The United Nations has expressed concern over police tactics during nationwide student protests in France, where more than 6,800 people have been detained and several injured as demonstrations over underfunded schools enter their third week.
Although most high schools had reopened by Friday, student unions vowed to continue their campaign, arguing that government concessions fall short of demands for more teachers, better classrooms and improved learning conditions.
The protests have attracted tens of thousands of people, university students, teachers and other supporters.
“We are following with concern incidents related to the student protests and high school blockades in France, some of which have turned violent,” Shabia Mantoo, spokesperson for the U.N. human rights office, said Friday.
She urged all sides to keep demonstrations peaceful and warned against the disproportionate use of force by law enforcement, stressing that the right to peaceful assembly must be upheld.
The demonstrations began in late September, with students complaining of teacher shortages, overloaded timetables, deteriorating school buildings and classrooms struggling to cope with rising temperatures.
Police have used tear gas, batons, stun grenades and water cannon to disperse blockades, prompting accusations of excessive force from students and rights groups. Police have opened 18 internal investigations into alleged misconduct.
A 15-year-old student lost a hand Monday after police fired a stun grenade, prompting the government to suspend the weapon’s use.
The Justice Ministry said Friday that more than 6,800 people had been detained since the protests began, with minors accounting for 86% of those arrested.
While most demonstrations have remained peaceful, some have involved vandalism, fires and clashes with police. Authorities reported attacks on education staff and damage to public property, while a school in the western city of Poitiers was set on fire.
The government made its first significant concession late Thursday, when Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced that about 3,000 qualified teachers who have yet to begin working would be deployed to address staffing shortages at the 114 high schools most affected.
The measure takes effect immediately and will cost several dozen million euros, Geffray told broadcaster TF1.
Student unions welcomed the announcement but insisted that it did not resolve the wider problems facing schools.
Marius Mesnil, a high school student union representative, said the decision showed that continued protests could deliver results.
“I find it crazy we need to block hundreds of high schools just to get a vacancy plan,” he told Franceinfo radio.
Mesnil described the offer as insufficient and called for another nationwide wave of school strikes Tuesday.
Other students expressed similar frustration. A 16-year-old in Toulouse said that protesters were saving their energy for the following week, while Alice, a student in Marseille, called the announcement a first step but said more action was needed.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has promised a broader plan to address the crisis by the end of October. Economy Minister Roland Lescure has also said there is room to consider education demands despite constraints in the proposed 2027 budget.
Under the current draft, education funding would rise 1.4% to 90.9 billion euros, the second-largest increase among government spending categories after defense.
The Education Ministry reported that 141 of France’s roughly 3,700 high schools remained closed Friday, down from about 800 a week earlier. However, disruptions continued at universities and other institutions.
Police cleared a blockade at Assas University, one of France’s leading law schools, in central Paris on Friday. Nearby Mines Paris, an elite engineering school, was also affected, while the Institut Catholique moved classes online because of a campus blockade.
Paris has become a focal point of the unrest, with students barricading school entrances and confronting riot police.
At Helene Boucher High School in northeastern Paris, students blocked the entrance with garbage bins Thursday before police moved in with tear gas. Demonstrators later gathered around Place de la Republique and Place de la Bastille, carrying signs demanding more education funding and questioning police conduct.
Some placards read “More money for repression than for our education” and “Who protects us from the police?”
Police used tear gas and water cannon to disperse crowds, while some protesters threw projectiles at officers.
Emma Khelil, an 18-year-old university student who returned to her former high school to support the movement, said she feared police violence.
“We’re here to defend our rights, not to lose an eye or a hand,” she told The Associated Press.
Khelil also described poor school conditions, including water leaks and insulation problems, and said she had occasionally seen rats inside the building.
Dounia Gergeon, a 39-year-old school librarian who joined a demonstration in Paris, said students felt abandoned and worried about their futures.
“They do not feel supported,” she said. “They feel cornered and forced to work under these conditions.”
Lecornu condemned attacks on students, school staff and police officers, along with fires, vandalism and thousands of hours of lost instruction. He accused political leaders of exploiting public anger for electoral purposes ahead of France’s presidential election in April.
“We cannot play with the safety of France’s youth,” he said.
The protests have intensified scrutiny of France’s public spending priorities as the government tries to address education shortages while reducing public debt.
Nearly 10% of teaching hours at French state high schools go unstaffed, according to education ministry figures. The shortages have fueled dissatisfaction among families, with some wealthier parents moving their children to private schools.
Stéphane Boujnah, head of Euronext, which operates the Paris stock market, said France needed difficult spending decisions to protect younger generations from the consequences of mounting debt. He suggested that reducing pension spending could free up money for education.
The Interior Ministry said 71,500 people demonstrated across France Thursday. Student and teacher unions are planning further strikes, raising the prospect of renewed disruption despite the decline in school closures.
The unrest has also coincided with demonstrations and labor action elsewhere in Europe.
In Belgium, two major labor unions organized a nationwide strike Friday that disrupted public transport, schools and air traffic over planned budget cuts and the rising cost of living. Tens of thousands were expected to attend a demonstration in Brussels.
Student protests have also spread across Belgium, with demonstrators demanding more teachers, smaller classes and improvements to school facilities. In Liège, authorities banned public gatherings until Oct. 16 after clashes involving tear gas and water cannon. Nearly 90 people were arrested, and several police officers were injured.
In Italy, students have occupied schools and organized marches over deteriorating buildings, education funding and increased military spending. Activists have explicitly drawn inspiration from the French movement, adopting the slogan “Let’s do as they do in France.”

articles.title: South Africa scraps asylum directive after anti-immigrant violence
articles.summary: South Africa’s government has withdrawn a directive requiring refugee reception offices to process more asylum applications after protests against the policy turned violent, leavin...
articles.full_text:
South Africa’s government has withdrawn a directive requiring refugee reception offices to process more asylum applications after protests against the policy turned violent, leaving at least 24 vehicles burned, shops looted and public safety concerns mounting in Johannesburg and Durban.
The Home Affairs Department announced Friday that it was scrapping the directive after its implementation triggered overcrowding at refugee offices and intensified tensions between anti-immigration demonstrators and foreign nationals.
The department said the directive had led to “serious consequences,” with offices overwhelmed within days, officials placed at risk and threats to public safety and order emerging.
“The Department will embark on a fresh process,” it said.
The withdrawal followed violence Thursday in Johannesburg’s Soweto township and Durban, a coastal city in KwaZulu-Natal province, where protesters opposed the government’s handling of asylum applications following a Constitutional Court ruling.
Acting National Police Commissioner Lt. Gen. Puleng Dimpane said 10 vehicles were torched in Soweto and 14 in Durban. Three foreign nationals were arrested in Durban in connection with an alleged assault on a South African protester.
“The right to raise concerns and to protest does not give anyone the right to commit crime,” Dimpane said, adding that police had reinforced public-order deployments in areas experiencing unrest.
In Soweto, violence broke out near a Home Affairs office in Orlando West, where several burned-out vehicles lined the streets. Metro police spokesperson Xolani Fihla said no injuries had been reported and officers were investigating whether additional vehicles had been set alight.
Fihla said police received reports of shots fired toward protesters, prompting retaliatory vehicle burnings. He did not identify who allegedly fired the shots or who owned the vehicles.
“The situation is a bit tense, but it has died down from the earlier violence that we did see during the day,” he said.
Community leader Tshepo Mposula said the demonstration began peacefully outside the Home Affairs office before some residents moved to close convenience stores owned by foreign nationals.
Mposula alleged that foreign nationals fired shots, angering protesters and prompting them to set vehicles ablaze. He said the demonstration was intended to remain peaceful.
“It was not supposed to escalate to this level. This was supposed to be a peaceful demonstration,” he said.
Fihla said police remained deployed as tensions continued and roads stayed closed. He acknowledged that officers initially monitoring the march lacked specialized public-order training and equipment.
“We couldn’t predict that this type of situation would happen,” he said.
In Durban, riot police were deployed to the city center as reports emerged of looting at shops owned by foreign nationals. The South African Broadcasting Corp. reported the looting, while smoke rose over parts of downtown as firefighters battled blazes, including a fire at a municipal building.
KwaZulu-Natal police spokesperson Col. Robert Netshiunda told SABC that three foreign nationals had been arrested on suspicion of attacking a South African protester and breaking the person’s neck. He said the incident may have triggered the unrest.
The violence followed months of demonstrations against undocumented immigration, with protesters demanding the deportation of foreigners living in South Africa illegally.
The unrest also reflects tensions surrounding a July ruling by the Constitutional Court, which struck down procedural barriers that had prevented some people from applying for asylum.
The restrictions affected people who entered South Africa irregularly, lacked asylum transit visas or missed deadlines for reporting to authorities. The court found that the barriers were unconstitutional, opening the way for more people to have their asylum claims considered.
Following the ruling, the Home Affairs Department instructed refugee reception offices to accept applications from people previously excluded by those procedures. Officials later acknowledged that they had been unprepared for the number of applicants who came forward.
The government’s Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration held an urgent briefing Thursday to address overcrowding and the challenges facing refugee reception offices.
“We confirm that all refugee offices were overwhelmed by the numbers of those coming for applications,” the committee said after meeting Wednesday night.
Authorities had pledged to expand processing capacity, accelerate decisions and strengthen identity checks. They also stressed that the court ruling did not automatically grant refugee status or permanent residence. It allowed applicants to have their claims assessed.
The department’s decision to withdraw the directive signals a change in how the government intends to manage the influx of asylum applications, although it has not yet detailed the fresh process it plans to introduce.
South Africa, the continent’s largest economy, has long attracted migrants seeking employment and better opportunities. However, the country has experienced recurring outbreaks of xenophobic violence for nearly two decades, often fueled by allegations that foreign nationals compete with South Africans for jobs, housing and public services.
The tensions have intensified ahead of local government elections scheduled for Nov. 4, with unemployment exceeding 30% adding to public frustration.
At least four foreign nationals were killed in violence earlier this year, according to South African police, although some African governments reported higher death tolls.
The unrest has also prompted thousands of foreign nationals to leave the country. Zimbabweans and Malawians accounted for the largest numbers of departures, while nationals of Ghana, Kenya, Lesotho, Mozambique, Nigeria and Uganda also fled.
Some were repatriated by their governments, adding to diplomatic tensions with Pretoria.
